# The Trump Administration Is Disappearing Immigrants and Asylum Seekers in Growing Third Country Removal Campaign


Through shadowy deportation agreements, the Trump administration is sending detained individuals to countries where they have no ties — and may face persecution.


[Sarah Mehta](https://www.aclu.org/bios/sarah-mehta) ,
ACLU


**Share This Page**


September 15, 2026


The Trump administration has deported[over 23,000 people](https://www.thirdcountrydeportationwatch.org/) over the last year and a half to countries they have no relationship with, where they may not speak the language, and where they generally have no legal status. Sometimes, it deports people to conflict zones or countries where they are likely to face persecution or even torture.


The Trump administration is spending tens of millions of dollars to fly people, shackled at times for[over 50 hours](https://www.humanrightsfirst.org/library/ice-flight-monitor-ice-air-flights-reach-record-high-removal-numbers-including-forced-third-country-transfers-in-april-2026-as-trump-administration-escalates-mass-deportation-campaign) , to “third countries” where they have no ties — even when they have won protection in U.S. immigration courts. The policies and agreements behind third country deportations are being negotiated behind closed doors, and some have never been made public.


On the one hand, what the U.S. government is really paying for is propaganda: The goal is to terrify immigrants into abandoning their cases and “self-deporting.” But at the same time, this administration is keeping its agreements, flight plans, and any information on who it has deported where and why as closely-held secrets. The secrecy is a strategy, and as we have seen with other regimes that participate in enforced disappearances, it is designed to hide these flights from court and public intervention, torment those on the flights, and terrify others waiting to find out if they will be next.


## What Are Third Country Deportations?


The U.S. government is deporting people who cannot be returned to their countries of origin to third countries. In many cases, these are individuals who suffered torture or persecution in their countries of origin, and now the U.S. government is trying to find other places where they can be deported instead. This summer, the Trump administration accelerated its deportations of immigrants from Latin America, Central Asia, and the Middle East to a growing list of countries including Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea, and the Central African Republic that are being paid by the United States through obscure deals. Since June, for example, the U.S. has sent three deportation flights to the Central African Republic (CAR), deporting Afghans, Russians, Jordanians, Iranians and many others. And yet, the U.S. State Department[warns](https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/central-african-republic.html) CAR is too dangerous to visit, but if you do, make a will and leave a DNA sample to identify your body.

### Immigrants' Rights


The U.S. government is spending at times $50 million per flight to deport people to third countries to[terrify](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/commentary/us-third-country-deportation-agreements-are-more-about-fear-numbers) them into giving up hope, abandoning their families, and self-deporting. Otherwise, they face what is effectively an[enforced disappearance](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-convention-protection-all-persons-enforced) to a country, even a continent, they’ve never seen. People deported to third countries have been held under house arrest or even in[prisons](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/12/magazine/deportation-immigrants-prison-eswatini.html) , with no pending criminal charges. There are now several reports of people deported to[Equatorial Guinea](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/equatorial-guinea-police-pull-guns-migrants-deported-by-trump-witnesses-say-2026-09-08/) being assaulted and threatened by armed guards. They have no permanent legal status and often have no identification documents, money, or support once deported.


What makes this Machiavellian plan especially cruel is who it targets: people who won protection in U.S. courts after proving they were likely to be persecuted or tortured if deported back to the countries they fled.[Khalil](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/29/us/afghans-deported-us-central-african-republic.html) , for example, is a young Afghan whose father and siblings helped the U.S. military in Afghanistan. After his family was attacked by the Taliban, he tried to seek safety in the United States, where a judge found he would likely be persecuted if returned to Afghanistan. Rather than release him to his family in the United States, the government then deported him to CAR, a conflict zone where Russian mercenaries provide the “security” and Muslims are often[targets](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/03/1160801) of violence.


Khalil’s case isn’t the exception; it’s the Trump administration’s model. Over the last several months, the United States has deported an[Iranian pro-democracy activist](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/us-deports-iranian-pro-democracy-activist-central-african-republic-lawyer-says-2026-06-12/) to CAR, a woman from Togo fleeing[genital mutilation](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/05/10/trump-third-country-deportations-ghana-togo/) to Ghana, and a[Nigerian man](https://www.newsweek.com/judge-slams-ice-deportation-of-man-tortured-by-his-government-12386058) tortured by Boko Haram to Ghana. In both of the latter cases, Ghana then deported the individuals back to the countries they had protection from. We hear routinely about people who won protection on account of their[LGBTQ status](https://immigrationequality.org/reports/protected-by-u-s-courts-deported-into-danger-new-immigration-equality-report-exposes-danger-to-lgbtq-immigrants-under-trump-administration-june-2026/) and are now deported to countries like[Cameroon](https://apnews.com/article/trump-deportation-cameroon-morocco-lgbt-interview-1ea278f4c981df798773e26972c5d54f) and[Ghana](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/jun/01/ghana-new-law-criminalising-lgbtq-activity) where that status is criminalized. These are people who have already endured horrors and cannot safely return home. Our government is using their suffering as an example of what immigrants will face if they don’t self-deport while claiming that these countries have given[diplomatic assurances](https://www.aclu.org/cases/diplomatic-assurances-foia) that immigrants will be safe there — assurances that the government knows are, in fact, baseless.


## The Secrecy Around Deportation Agreements


In January 2025, the United States had no third country deportation agreements. Today, the U.S. government has signed more than 35, with the exact number still unknown. There are now numerous cases of people deported to third countries under this scheme who have also then been deported onwards to the very countries they fled in what is known as chain refoulement, which is in violation of human rights law.


But while the government is deliberating broadcasting its general plans in order to coerce people into self-deporting, the Trump administration is also hiding specific details about its agreements, including who is being targeted for third country removal, to avoid scrutiny and public outcry.


In many cases, agreements between the United States and the receiving country are only publicly announced days before a deportation flight takes off. The agreement with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, was[signed](https://www.state.gov/droc-26-328) in February 2026 but only made public in[April](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/congo-says-it-will-receive-third-country-deportees-from-the-u-s-under-new-deal) , shortly before the[first](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/first-deportees-us-arrive-congo-capital-sources-say-2026-04-17/) third country flight. Agreements with some repeat players like Mexico have never been made public; part of Ghana’s was just published this September, over a year after it was signed. This lack of transparency undercuts public and congressional oversight, fueling a system where people are deported in secret to horrific conditions with no accountability.


The flights are also a closely guarded secret, making it virtually impossible for detained individuals to find attorneys and contest their deportation to a place where they may face persecution or torture. The government’s secrecy appears to be a calculated attempt to rush people out of the country before court intervention and before the media or Congress can corroborate who is on the flights.

### J.G.G. v. TRUMP


**Status:** Ongoing


[J.g.g. V. Trump. Explore Case.](https://www.aclu.org/cases/j-g-g-v-trump)


Last year, under the wartime Alien Enemies Act, the U.S. government illegally deported more than 100 people to El Salvador where they were detained and tortured at the infamous Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT. During an emergency court hearing on March 15, 2025, where the ACLU sought a temporary restraining order, government counsel repeatedly told a federal court that counsel was not aware of any immediate plans to deport these men. In fact, two of the planes took off during the hearing. At the end of the hearing, the court[ordered](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/22/alien-enemies-act-james-boasberg-ruling-00704244) the government to return the planes and not disembark them in El Salvador, whether they had taken off or not. While aware of the court order, the Trump administration ordered the flights to continue on to El Salvador and later claimed it could not bring the deported individuals back. The litigation[continues](https://www.aclu.org/cases/j-g-g-v-trump) , with hearings proceeding in September in federal court, to ensure due process for these individuals and to hold the government accountable for defying court orders.


## Attorneys, Reporters, and Public Intentionally Left in the Dark


Hiding these flights was a deliberate strategy. To this day, the U.S. government continues to hide its third country deportation plans, particularly to places where people face danger. We routinely hear from attorneys that the government will not confirm where or when it might deport their clients, has even denied imminent plans to deport specific individuals who are already on the planes, and has allegedly lied to immigrants and their attorneys about the flight destination.


This secrecy is working for the government: It means that people cannot get lawyers in time, and reporters cannot obtain any official information about these deportation flights until the planes land. It means people cannot prepare for or challenge their deportation — and the public doesn’t know what has happened until it is too late. We may never know the full scope of what the United States is offering countries in exchange for taking our neighbors, and we may never get a full accounting of who has been disappeared. But what we are learning every week is that the dangers people face when deported, at taxpayer expense, are predictable, escalating, and intentionally cruel.

### New ACLU Report Sounds the Alarm on How Trump Administration’s Mass Deportation Agenda is Eroding Democracy


WASHINGTON — The American Civil Liberties Union today released a new report, 76 Ways Mass Deportation is Breaking Our Democracy, detailing how the Trump administration is using mass deportation as the pretext and mechanism to attack civil liberties and structural democratic safeguards at an unparalleled scale and speed. The report comes as Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests have hit a record high, as the Trump administration has shifted its approach from mass raids to more discrete arrests following widespread outrage. From the deployment of federal agents and military troops for immigration enforcement in U.S. cities, to the mass revocation of visas and other forms of lawful status, and the targeting of immigrants’ rights protesters, the Trump administration has repeatedly used immigration policy as a trojan horse for attacks on core pillars of U.S. democracy. Notably, the report categorizes the dizzying array of abuses into three major categories, which often overlap: Attacks on civil rights and liberties, as the Trump administration has used mass deportations as both a pretext and distraction for its assault on myriad constitutional rights – including the rights to free speech and freedom of assembly and due process – impacting citizens and noncitizens alike. Attacks on democratic checks and balances, as the administration expands its federal deportation police and executive power, eviscerating due process for immigrants and normalizing ICE’s violence, while evading and even defying court orders. Attacks on multiracial, pluralistic democracy, as the administration continues to gut existing legal protections and introduce new policies targeting people who are immigrants – including through visa and entry bans and efforts to end birthright citizenship and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) – in what appears to be a calculated attempt to change the racial makeup of the U.S. now and into the future. “For the past year and a half, the ACLU and advocates have warned that the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda pulls straight from an authoritarian playbook – and now, we’re seeing the devasting impacts of those policies, with citizens and noncitizens alike paying the price and the state of our democracy in crisis,” said Naureen Shah, director of immigration policy and government affairs at the ACLU. “This report is a clarion call to members of Congress to strengthen and repair our pluralistic, multiracial democracy by passing meaningful immigration reforms. That must include creating a broad path to citizenship for immigrants who contribute to our communities and our economy.” Within the report, the ACLU also calls on members of Congress to restore and defend democratic rights and norms through transformative immigration reform, including by creating a broad path to citizenship and modernization of border processing and policies. It also calls on lawmakers to build stronger accountability, transparency and oversight measures to effectively compel the executive branch to uphold civil rights and civil liberties. “From the cancellation of Congressionally mandated protections like TPS to the arrest of noncitizen students for exercising their First Amendment rights, the Trump administration has repeatedly violated bedrock democratic principles under the guise of immigration enforcement,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy and government affairs at the ACLU. “As this administration has shown, no one is safe from its extreme mass deportation agenda. Our elected officials – and the state of our democracy – cannot afford to allow this lawlessness to continue. The time to act is now.” This report is the fourth in the ACLU’s affirmative immigration vision series, in which policy and legal experts explore how the Trump administration’s immigration agenda has harmed communities nationwide, undermined our democracy, and wreaked havoc on key industries and weakened the American workforce. The series will also outline steps that members of Congress, as well as state and local policymakers, can take to reform the U.S. immigration system and inoculate against future attacks on core rights and safety. You can read the full report here: https://www.aclu.org/publications/76-ways-mass-deportation-is-breaking-our-democracy
